title: Stateless-to-Stateful Migration and Cutover Guidelines for Private Deploys
author: Marcus Chen
content:
Summary

This document provides a field-proven, end-to-end set of guidelines for migrating Redwood private deploys from a primarily stateless serving topology to deployments that include stateful components (local KV cache, model shard state, persistent orchestrator metadata). It focuses on cutover choreography, minimizing latency/regression risk to customer traffic, and safe rollback strategies. Intended audience: deploy engineers, SREs, field ops, and customer engineering.

Goals

- Ensure zero-or-minimal customer-visible downtime during cutover.
- Maintain inference SLOs (p95 latency targets) during migration windows.
- Provide deterministic rollback steps with evidence preservation for compliance.
- Document ownership boundaries, test gates, and telemetry checks required for safe progression.

When to use this guide

Use this playbook when:
1) A private deployment introduces local persistent state (e.g., on-node KV cache, persistent model shard indexes, local metadata stores).
2) Existing topology is stateless (requests routed to ephemeral inference workers) and will transition to hybrid or stateful nodes.
3) Customers require controlled cutover with audit/evidence preservation.

Prerequisites and assumptions

- Customer acceptance of a short maintenance window (if required).
- Admin access to control plane and worker nodes.
- Backups enabled for any persistence targets (see backups checklist).
- Canary environment that mirrors production networking and routing rules.
- Observability instrumentation: request tracing, token-level latency, KV hit/miss, model shard health.

Checklist (pre-cutover)

Table: Pre-cutover verification
- Ownership and schedule: Confirm primary contacts and maintenance window.
- Backups: Last full snapshot available and verified (timestamp + checksum).
- Canary tests: Canary run passing (success rate >= 99% over 30m).
- Capacity: Node pool headroom >= 20% for the cutover period.
- Alerts: Pager and oncall engaged; suppression rules prepared for planned alarms.

Detailed workflow

1) Prepare canary environment (dry-run)
   - Clone deployment config to a canary control plane namespace. Use the exact quantization/model binary used in prod.
   - Run a 2-stage canary: single-tenant functional verification, then multi-tenant traffic replay.
   - Verify metrics: token throughput, p95/p99 latency, KV hit rate >= expected baseline.

2) Stage persistent storage and seeding
   - Create persistent volumes and attach to target nodes.
   - Seed KV cache from snapshot: run snapshot restore with index hash verification. Example CLI: redwoodctl kv restore --from s3://backups/<snapshot> --target nodepool-a --verify-hash
   - Validate seed by running a deterministic probe suite that checks 100 representative prefixes.

3) Introduce hybrid nodes behind a controlled routing policy
   - Bring up stateful nodes but keep them opt-in (no traffic) by default.
   - Use routing flagging: set node label stateful=true but route weight=0.
   - Run health checks and ensure these nodes report READY with no serving traffic.

4) Warm-up and KV priming
   - Execute a staged priming job: prefix-based synthetic requests that exercise common KV keys and model shard hot paths.
   - Monitor KV hit rate and backend egress. Goal: KV warm-up should stabilize within expected priming duration (document expected minutes/hours per deployment size).

5) Canary traffic shift (small percentage)
   - Shift 1–5% of production traffic to hybrid nodes using traffic steering rules in the control plane.
   - Monitor: error rate (5xx), model correctness checks (see validation below), latency p95/p99, and resource metrics (GPU utilization, disk I/O).
   - Hold for observation window: recommended 30–60 minutes for low-risk changes, 2–3 hours for large customers.

6) Progressive ramp to full capacity
   - If canary looks good, increase traffic progressively: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%. Each step has a mandatory observation window.
   - Use automated rollback gates: if error rate exceeds threshold or latency breach for more than 3 consecutive windows, traffic reverts to stateless nodes automatically.

Validation and correctness checks

A. Functional correctness
- Use curated prompt set containing edge cases (length, tokenization differences, stateful continuity checks).
- Run A/B comparisons: compare outputs from stateless vs stateful for the same prefixes and quantify divergence. Pass criteria: divergence rate <= agreed tolerance (typically 0.5–2% depending on customer).

B. Performance SLOs
- p95 latency must not regress by more than configured tolerance (default 20%).
- Token throughput per GPU within expected margin.

C. Telemetry and evidence collection
- Persist logs and traces with cutover tag for audit (cutover_id=<YYYYMMDD>-<site>-<id>).
- Snapshot control plane state and store checksums in the evidence bucket.

Automated rollback design

Trigger conditions (examples)
- 5xx error spike: sustained > 1% of requests for 10 minutes.
- Latency breach: p95 > target * 1.25 for 3 consecutive windows.
- Functional regression: A/B divergence above tolerance.

Rollback actions
1) Immediate traffic switch: Reset routing weights to route 100% to stateless nodes.
2) Quarantine stateful nodes: disable new writes and set read-only where applicable.
3) Preserve evidence: capture disk snapshots and control plane export.
4) Post-rollback validation: run smoke tests for basic traffic flow and customer-facing checks.

Cutover emergency playbook (critical path)

- Situation: Unrecoverable degradation detected post-cutover.
- Owners oncall: primary oncall (SRE), deployment lead, customer success lead.
- Steps: 1) Execute automated rollback. 2) Notify customer using predefined templates. 3) Gather evidence and open an incident ticket with severity S1. 4) If rollback fails, escalate to engineering platform leads and consider network-level diversion (BGP/edge).

Data consistency and reconciliation

- For KV caches that are eventually consistent: define a TTL and drift tolerance. Provide a reconciliation job that runs after cutover to reconcile hot keys from upstream storage. Example cron job: redwoodctl reconcile-kv --target nodepool-a --window 2h --verify
- For metadata stores: maintain write-ahead logs for the first 24–72 hours after cutover to allow replay to original nodes if needed.

Configuration examples

Sample routing policy (YAML snippet):

routingPolicy: |
  - name: hybrid-canary
    selector: "label:stateful=true"
    weight: 5
    observationWindow: 30m
    rollbackOn: ["error_rate>0.01","p95>latency_target*1.25"]

Agent command examples

- Start priming job: redwoodctl jobs create --script priming/prefix-prime.yaml --namespace canary
- Snapshot verify: redwoodctl snapshot verify --path s3://evidence/backups/2026-01-11.snap
- Shift weight: redwoodctl routing set-weight --policy hybrid-canary --weight 20

Owners and escalation matrix

- Deployment lead: Marcus Chen (eng-private-deployments)
- SRE oncall: see team rota (link to rota)
- Customer success escalation: Priya Nair
- Engineering platform: Sofia Morales

Post-cutover activities

- 24h watch: Maintain elevated telemetry retention and daily sync calls for the first 24 hours.
- 7-day reconciliation: Run full-data reconciliation and performance baseline reporting.
- Retrospective: Create a cutover postmortem within 72 hours, include mitigations and TTR metrics.

Risk matrix and mitigation examples

- Risk: Cold-start latency on stateful nodes -> Mitigation: aggressive priming and staggered warm-up.
- Risk: Stateful write conflicts -> Mitigation: read-only mode during initial ramp and write-ahead logs.
- Risk: Traffic oscillation -> Mitigation: route dampening and minimum observation windows.

Appendix A: Backup and evidence preservation checklist

1) Control plane snapshot (JSON) with timestamp and checksum.
2) Persistent volume snapshot (cloud or SAN) and retention policy.
3) KV snapshot exported to evidence bucket.
4) Trace logs with cutover_id tag exported.

Appendix B: Minimal smoke test suite (commands)

- Validate endpoints: curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://<edge>/v1/health | jq
- Sample inference probe: echo '{"input":"Hello world"}' | redwoodctl invoke --model <model-version> --timeout 10s
- A/B comparer: redwoodctl compare --left stateless --right hybrid --inputs testset/edgecases.json --threshold 0.02

Notes and references

- This playbook complements our incremental stateful upgrade strategy. See related design doc for long-term migration patterns.
- Keep this document updated with new failure modes discovered during postmortems.
